Kratom (Mitragynia speciosa Korth) is a tree-like plant native to Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and other parts of southeast Asia. Indigenous users create a “juice” by boiling fresh kratom leaves for several hours that is then diluted with hot water to make kratom tea. Kratom is used in traditional environments to treat diarrhea, hypertension, cough, fever, impotence, and other ailments. Kratom is used by manual laborers for its mild stimulant effects, a replacement remedy for individuals with problematic opioid use, and as a mild analgesic agent. In the west, many different kratom formulations are available, including tinctures, extracts, capsules, softgels, concentrated products, as well as dried leaf powders and cut leaf material. 5

December 18, 2025 Page 6 Kratom in western countries is most commonly used as a remedy for opioid addiction, chronic pain, depression, and anxiety. 19. The neurobehavioral effects of kratom are more subtle than the commonly described stimulant effects at low doses and opioid effects at higher doses. Low doses of kratom increase alertness, energy, and talkativeness. At doses greater than 5 grams, however, kratom users describe the persistence of heightened alertness coupled with analgesia. These effects account for the use of kratom as a mild stimulant for manual laborers, a replacement remedy for individuals with problematic opioid use, and as a mild analgesic agent. 20. Some of the biological effects of kratom arise from binding of alkaloidal components to a number of neurotransmitter receptors in the central nervous system, including the µ-opioid (MOR), κ-opioid, serotonergic (5-HT), and alpha (α1) receptors, among others. MOR activity is particularly important. MOR activation mediates pain, respiratory rate, gastrointestinal transit time, nausea, and pruritis, among other effects. Each of these effects is mediated via distinct signaling pathways following binding of an agonist to the MOR receptor. 21. Classical opioid agonists (e.g., morphine and fentanyl) are “unbiased” agonists in that they indiscriminately activate all biological effects mediated by MOR. Kratom is different. The most prevalent—and best studied—alkaloid in kratom is mitragynine. In contrast to classical unbiased MOR agonists, mitragynine is a “biased” agonist in that it produces some, but not all, effects that arise from receptor binding of a classical MOR agonist such as morphine or fentanyl. 22. For example, while mitragynine produces analgesia, it does not produce the stupor characteristic of classic, unbiased MOR agonists. Instead, kratom produces increased alertness. Furthermore, mitragynine does not produce the respiratory depression that is a leading cause of mortality from classical unbiased MOR agonist overdose (Macko 1972; Varadi 2016; Kruegel 2019; Boyer 2012). 23. In fact, the clinical features as well as the time course of the toxidrome from kratom has never been described. Testing for mitragynine is generally limited to commercial forensic companies and medical examiner offices. Mitragynine itself undergoes postmortem redistribution; the postmortem concentration of mitragynine measured by forensic laboratories is over three times higher than premortem blood. 24. In general, adverse events attributed to kratom have been derived from database studies, poorly controlled case reports, or small case series, each of which has serious deficiencies in patient background information, including medical, social, or family history; clinical evaluation; scene findings; or analytical technique. These poorly controlled studies at times associate kratom with agitation, seizures, liver injury, renal injury, ventricular dysrhythmia, and respiratory depression. Individually and collectively, these studies lack the scientific heft to establish causation between kratom use and any adverse event. 25. For example, case reports describing right ventricular failure in the setting of intermittent kratom ingestions are complicated by the distant use of kratom, the lack of clarity 6

Case Synopsis 27. Harmony Moller had no known significant issues in her medical history, though she used cannabis and ethanol. 28. On or about February 5, 2023, she complained that she did not feel well and developed vomiting. The next day, Ms. Moller collapsed and was found by her mother (Kathleen Moller), who called 911. First responders found Ms. Moller in cardiac arrest. Paramedics intubated Ms. Moller and administered naloxone with no effect. Paramedics made a field declaration of death. 29. Ms. Moller’s autopsy was performed on February 8, 2023. The examining pathologist identified areas of nutmeg liver “consistent with chronic passive congestion.” In thorax, the bronchi contained blood, and the pathologist noted that the “[p]ulmonary cut surfaces demonstrate hemorrhage, congestion, and edema.” From her heart, the pulmonic valve was harvested for transplant, but the remainder was not used (St. Tammany Parish Coroner Records). 30. Ms. Moller’s heart was shipped to the Jesse E Edwards Registry of Cardiovascular Disease in St Paul, MN. Pathologists at that facility identified an enlarged heart (cardiomegaly) with hypertrophy of both ventricles (mild biventricular hypertrophy) with mild dilation of the right ventricle. In the left ventricle, the pathologist identified that the left coronary artery “arises 5 mm above the left sinotubular ridge with an acute angle of origin. There is an inferior aortic wall flap over the origin of the left coronary artery.” (Jesse E Edwards Registry of Cardiovascular Disease records). In addition, the left ventricular wall was thickened at 15 mm and the intraventricular septum was 17 mm. 31. On microscopy, pathologists noted hypertrophy of atrial and ventricular myocytes, with increased right ventricular interstitial and perivascular fibrosis. The posterior wall of the right ventricle contained hypertrophic myocytes. While the AV node was normal, the ventricular septum and the lateral wall of the left ventricle are hypertrophic with scattered hypereosinophilic myocytes. Interstitial and perivascular fibrosis were present. The anterior wall of the left ventricle had hypertrophic myocytes with interstitial and perivascular fibrosis. 32. Postmortem analyses were performed by two different laboratories. National Medical Laboratories measured a mitragynine concentration of 150 ng/mL, along with caffeine, naloxone, cannabis/metabolites, diphenhydramine, and promethazine (NMS Laboratories 7

No evidence supports the contention that Harmony Moller’s use of kratom contributed to her death. The postmortem concentration of mitragynine identified in Ms. Moller’s blood was 158 ng/mL as measured by the Gerona lab (St. Tammany Parish Coroner records); commercial clinical laboratories measured the mitragynine concentration as 150 ng/mL (St. Tammany Parish Coroner records). Mitragynine undergoes postmortem redistribution, a process where the concentration of a substance changes following death. The available scientific literature demonstrates that the postmortem concentration of mitragynine is approximately triple that of pre- mortem measurements (Osawa 2025). To a reasonable degree of medical certainty, therefore, Ms. Moller’s premortem concentration of mitragynine was approximately 50 ng/mL, a value that occurred in human clinical trials involving kratom. Notably, none of the participants in these studies developed cardiac toxicity, much less a life-threatening event. Ms. Moller did not die from her kratom use. 76. In fact, medical examiners initially noted that the cause of death was “chronic liver congestion.” Chronic liver congestion is a medical condition often associated with right heart failure; backup of blood (i.e., “congestion”) into the liver produces fibrotic changes that become apparent even on visual inspection of the liver. Notably, kratom has not been associated with chronic liver congestion, even among patients where right heart failure was putatively associated with distant and undefined kratom ingestion (Alameh 2025). 77. Although I agree with the medical examiner’s finding that Ms. Moller died from complications of her unrecognized congenital heart disease—that has a recognized association with sudden cardiac death—I find that the medical examiner errs in failing to consider adequately the pharmacophysiology of the full range of substances identified on postmortem testing. 78. I find that the medical examiner errs in determining that Harmony Moller’s kratom use contributed to her death. In fact, the pharmacophysiology of kratom is more likely to be protective against cardiac sudden death in a patient such as Ms. Moller who had a high takeoff of the coronary artery with an acute angle of origin complicated by an inferior aortic flap. Following ingestion, mitragynine exerts parasympathetic effects on the cardiovascular system (Saengmolee 2022; Prevete 2024). These effects, measured generally as a slight decrease in systolic and diastolic blood pressure even in the setting of greater alertness, are insufficient to contribute to morbidity and mortality of an individual with high takeoff of the coronary artery with an acute angle of origin of the coronary artery complicated by an inferior aortic flap (Saengmolee 2022; Prevete 2024).1 79. I also find that the medical examiner errs in ignoring other substances more likely than mitragynine to worsen the congenital heart disease described in the medical record. Normally, the aorta has “elasticity,” meaning it can dilate slightly during a pulse of blood from the heart. Harmony Moller ingested caffeine. Caffeine is an over-the-counter stimulant that increases pulse rate and intra-aortic blood pressure, but caffeine also limits the elasticity (i.e., how much the blood vessel can expand in response to increased blood pressure) of the aorta. Caffeine’s pharmacologic actions make it dangerous in a person with high takeoff of the left coronary artery with an acute angle of origin. Caffeine increases aortic blood pressure and decreases aortic elasticity. These direct pharmacologic effects of caffeine compress the opening of the coronary artery precisely because the coronary artery has an acute angle of origin that narrows as the aorta expands (Virmani 1984). Moreover, the inferior aortic flap is an additional obstruction to blood flow into the coronary artery as the increased aortic blood pressure caused by caffeine presses it against the wall of the aorta. Ms. Moller’s caffeine use occluded the coronary artery and hindered blood flow into heart muscle. This decrease in cardiac perfusion caused a malignant arrhythmia culminating in sudden cardiac death. Caffeine, not mitragynine, exacerbated Ms. Moller’s congenital heart disease and contributed to her death. 80. Even if Ms. Moller was not taking her caffeine supplements, she also had “Mini Thins,” a weight-loss remedy. This product contains caffeine and yohimbine, among other plant products. Yohimbine is a presynaptic alpha-2 antagonist. The pharmacologic effects of yohimbine are to increase pulse rate and blood pressure. These direct pharmacologic effects of yohimbine, either with or without caffeine, compress the opening of the coronary artery precisely because the coronary artery has an acute angle of origin that narrows as the aorta expands (Virmani 1984). 81. Even if Harmony Moller did not die of her congenital heart disease complicated by her caffeine use, she had other, more plausible causes of death than mitragynine toxicity. For example, Ms. Moller’s vomiting was so severe that Kathleen Moller administered multiple antiemetics without improvement. Harmony Moller was taking two different caffeine-containing supplements. Caffeine is a methylxanthine. The methylxanthine toxidrome involves vomiting, seizure, and ventricular dysrthythmias (Shimane 2017). Death in methylxanthine-poisoned individuals arises from seizures or from malignant ventricular dysrhythmias (Shimane 2017; Poussel 2013). The medical examiner failed to quantify the postmortem concentration of caffeine even though Harmony Moller’s clinical presentation (i.e., severe vomiting despite multiple antiemetics before being found down with no anatomic cause of death other than her congenital heart disease) was consistent with lethal methylxanthine poisoning. This clinical presentation is also inconsistent with mitragynine toxicity. 82. Harmony Moller did not die from any contribution of mitragynine to her congenital heart disease. 83. Harmony Moller did not die from mitragynine toxicity 84. Harmony Moller did not die from her kratom use. 85. I am able to defend rigorously these conclusions, made within a reasonable degree of medical and toxicologic certainty. I have reviewed the report generated by Plaintiff’s expert Christopher Williams, PhD, a laboratory researcher and NIH-funded scientist. Dr. Williams acknowledges he cannot “identify cause of death” or provide “clinical diagnostic information.” 87. Dr. Williams attempts to link together all negative aspects of opioids, kratom and kratom alkaloids. He attempts unsuccessfully to establish a toxic profile of kratom alkaloids, each with an atypical corynanthe structure, by drawing parallels with formal opioids having phenanthrene, anilidopiperidine, and diphenylpropylamine chemical structures. 88. In formulating his opinions on the effects of kratom alkaloids on health, Dr. Williams picks and chooses among the scientific literature while making numerous scientific omissions and factual errors.
